topic: The Cloud Collapse: AWS vs Microsoft
description: A dramatic, numbers-first timeline of how enterprises rewired spending after the COVID surge—AWS stayed king early, while Microsoft Azure accelerated fast, especially from 2021–2023 as customers consolidated and migrated to higher-commitment contracts.
youtube_description:
🚨 AWS vs Azure isn’t just a rivalry—it’s an enterprise migration story written in contracts, cloud budgets, and customer consolidation. In this chart race, we track estimated annual cloud revenue by provider from 2015 to 2025—capturing the moment the “cloud build” became a “cloud run,” and the biggest platforms accelerated while smaller players shrank.

Chapters (timeline beats):
00:00 — 2015–2016: AWS already leads; Azure starts scaling from a small base
00:35 — 2017–2018: Enterprise workloads move from pilots to production
01:25 — 2019–2020: The COVID shock triggers a massive compute pull
02:10 — 2021: Azure’s jump mirrors migration waves and hybrid commitments
02:55 — 2022: Consolidation + cost controls favor the largest platforms
03:40 — 2023: The AI and data-center arms race reshapes budgets
04:25 — 2024: AWS pulls ahead again, but Azure narrows the gap
05:10 — 2025: Azure closes further; smaller clouds remain pressured

What to watch in the animation:
• AWS maintains dominance but faces faster share gain from Azure after 2021.
• Google Cloud grows more steadily, never achieving the same scale lift.
• IBM Cloud contracts as organizations shift away from smaller ecosystems.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The Cloud “Crash Landing” didn’t kill the giants—AWS and Azure *reassigned the map*.

In 2015, cloud was already real, but the numbers still felt early: AWS pulled in about $44B while Azure was only around $5B. Google Cloud hovered near $1.8B and IBM Cloud sat around $3.0B—small enough that most enterprises still treated migration like a project, not a platform.

Then 2016–2019 happened. AWS grew from $55B to $110B, building dominance with scale, reliability, and the services catalog customers couldn’t stop using. Azure also surged—from $10B to $55B—as Microsoft pushed hybrid integrations and enterprise contracts. By 2019, AWS was still clearly ahead, but Azure’s trajectory was already bending upward. Google remained incremental (about $10.5B in 2019), while IBM Cloud drifted (about $4.1B).

2020 was the shock: COVID spiked compute demand overnight. AWS jumped to roughly $140B. Azure climbed to about $70B. This is where the “cloud build” switched into “cloud run”—more workloads moved from experimentation to always-on systems.

But 2021 is the real drama. AWS went to about $200B, yet Azure accelerated harder to about $115B—closing the gap fast. In 2022, consolidation and cost controls favored the biggest ecosystems: AWS reached about $274B while Azure surged to about $190B. By 2023, AWS was around $290B and Azure about $220B—while Google stayed in the mid-$30Bs and IBM Cloud continued to shrink.

Fast-forward: 2024–2025. AWS lands at about $360B (2024) then ~$460B (2025). Azure rises to about $300B (2024) and ~$430B (2025)—closing even more. The “collapse” wasn’t a collapse of cloud. It was a collapse of *small ecosystems*.

AWS begins as the clear leader ($44B in 2015 rising to $110B by 2019) and benefits from early scale advantages. Azure starts far smaller ($5B in 2015) but accelerates dramatically from 2020 onward: as COVID-era demand expands compute, Azure rises from about $70B (2020) to roughly $115B (2021) and $190B (2022). The turning point is 2021–2022, when enterprise migration plus hybrid commitments translate into higher commitment spending and platform consolidation.

By 2023, AWS is around $290B and Azure about $220B—while Google Cloud grows more gradually and IBM Cloud contracts as many organizations shift toward larger ecosystems. The final stretch shows a near-reshaping of leadership: in 2024 AWS reaches about $360B while Azure hits about $300B, and by 2025 AWS is about $460B versus Azure about $430B.

Bottom line: the “cloud winners” aren’t just growing—they’re absorbing the spend that smaller players lose.

threads_caption:
Hot take: the “cloud collapse” wasn’t about cloud dying—it was about the market consolidating. 😮

Look at the swing from 2015 to 2025: AWS goes from ~$44B to ~$460B, while Azure goes from ~$5B to ~$430B. That’s not a normal growth story—that’s a *closing gap* story.

2021–2022 is where it gets wild: AWS hits about $200B then $274B, but Azure jumps to ~$115B then ~$190B. Meanwhile Google Cloud stays steady-ish (mid $30Bs by 2022–2023), and IBM Cloud keeps slipping (around $3–$4B).

So the dramatic part isn’t that cloud got destroyed—it’s that smaller ecosystems got squeezed out while AWS and Azure grabbed more of the enterprise budget.

Which side are you betting on for the next move: AWS dominance, Azure catch-up, or a surprise third player? 👇
